items.raw_excerpt:
Hi HN, I built AI Flag Bot to tackle the growing problem of AI-generated accounts flooding X (Twitter). How it works:
- Spot a suspicious post? Reply with @AIFlagBot flag to report it
- The community votes on whether it's AI-generated
- Votes are weighted by voter reputation, which goes up or down based on accuracy
- Once consensus is reached, the account gets added to a shared blocklist
- Paid subscribers get automatic blocking synced to their X account ($5/m to cover API costs) The reputation system is the core idea — voters who consistently identify AI accounts correctly gain more influence, while bad actors lose it. items.title: AI agent has more production access than your senior engineers
items.raw_excerpt: There’s a pattern I keep seeing across teams adopting AI agents for infrastructure, and it’s starting to scare me. A team sets up an agent to help with Terraform, Kubernetes configs, or cloud deployments. To make it useful, they give it cloud credentials, state files, sometimes CI/CD pipeline access. They test it in staging. It works. They move it to production. Nobody asks: what’s the blast radius if this thing gets prompt-injected? Coding agents are not infrastructure agents. The industry is conflating these two categories. We treat all AI agents as “AI-assisted development” and apply the same security model. But the threat surfaces are completely different. A coding agent operates in a sandbox (your IDE), produces artifacts that get reviewed (PRs), and has a natural checkpoint (CI/CD).

excerpt_i18n.en: The State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission (SASAC) of the State Council recently proposed that central enterprises should strengthen investment traction, actively expand effective investment in computing power, promote the coordinated development of "computing power + electricity," enhance the entire chain's data governance capabilities, and continuously consolidate the foundation of the artificial intelligence industry. At this meeting, SASAC called on central enterprises to reinforce independent innovation, focus on breaking through key core technologies, continuously tackle "large model" technology, and push more innovative achievements from prototypes to products and industries. They are also required to strengthen scenario cultivation, accurately align artificial intelligence with primary responsibilities, industrial needs, and make greater efforts in high compatibility, high value, and high reliability to promote large-scale application of AI. Additionally, SASAC requires central enterprises to strengthen open-source collaboration, accelerate the iteration and upgrade of the open-source "Renewal Community," strive to become "empowering enterprises," advance the construction of the "AI+" industrial community, and continuously foster a mutually beneficial and win-win industrial ecosystem. (Xinhua News Agency)

El 11 se informó que el Consejo de Administración del Consejo de Estado había celebrado recientemente una reunión para profundizar la implementación de la iniciativa especial "AI+" de las empresas estatales centrales. En esta reunión, el Consejo de Administración del Consejo de Estado propuso que las empresas estatales centrales fortalezcan la innovación autónoma, se esfuercen por superar tecnologías clave y nucleares, continúen atacando la tecnología de "grandes modelos" y promuevan que más resultados de innovación autónoma pasen de muestras a productos y se conviertan en industrias; deben fortalecer la formación de escenarios, mejorar la conexión precisa entre la inteligencia artificial y las responsabilidades principales y las necesidades de la industria, con alta adaptabilidad y alto valor.
